claim: Cell stretch and subsequent compression reshape the plasma membrane in a way that generates local membrane evaginations in the 100 nm scale.
source: We show that cell stretch and subsequent compression reshape the PM in a way that generates local membrane evaginations in the 100 nm scale.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data including TEM measurements showing evagination dimensions and fluorescence microscopy observations.

claim: Membrane evaginations generated by compression are recognized by I-BAR proteins.
source: These evaginations are recognized by I-BAR proteins, which triggers a burst of actin polymerization mediated by Rac1 and Arp2/3.
evidence: The claim is supported by APEX labeling experiments showing IRSp53 enrichment at evaginations and by experiments with IRSp53 mutants.

claim: Recognition of evaginations by I-BAR proteins triggers a burst of actin polymerization mediated by Rac1 and Arp2/3.
source: These evaginations are recognized by I-BAR proteins, which triggers a burst of actin polymerization mediated by Rac1 and Arp2/3.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing actin recruitment to evaginations, effects of Rac1 mutants, and CK-666 inhibition of Arp2/3.

claim: Actin polymerization re-flattens the evagination, completing a mechanochemical feedback loop.
source: The actin polymerization burst subsequently re-flattens the evagination, completing the mechanochemical feedback loop.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging showing evagination resorption and by inhibitor experiments showing that blocking actin polymerization impairs resorption.

claim: Normal human dermal fibroblasts subjected to 5% equibiaxial stretch increase their area by depleting plasma membrane reservoirs such as ruffles.
source: As previously described, when tensile stress was applied cells increased their area by depleting PM reservoirs, such as ruffles (Gauthier et al., 2012; Kosmalska et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work and by the experimental observations in the current study.

claim: After 3 minutes of stretch, release results in a compression stimulus that stores excess membrane in folds visualized as bright fluorescent spots of approximately 500 nm.
source: After 3 min, stretch was released, resulting in a compression stimulus. At this point, excess membrane was stored again in folds, visualized as bright fluorescent spots of ≈500 nm (Figure 1A and Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: Compression-induced spots incorporate approximately 1.5% of plasma membrane area.
source: These spots incorporate approximately 1.5% of PM area (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and thus store an important fraction of the area modified by cell stretch.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Compression-generated folds are formed passively by the plasma membrane to accommodate compression.
source: As we have previously published (Kosmalska et al., 2015), these spots are formed passively by the PM to accommodate compression, analogously to what occurs when compressing synthetic lipid bilayers (Staykova et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on cell compression and synthetic lipid bilayers.

claim: De-stretched cells display numerous bud-shaped evaginations at their apical plasma membrane side that correlate with bright spots seen by fluorescence.
source: De-stretched cells displayed numerous bud-shaped evaginations at their apical PM side that correlated with the bright spots seen by fluorescence (Figure 1B and C), showing that the PM bends outward (thereby minimizing friction with the underlying cortex).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlated SEM and fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: The plasma membrane bends outward in evaginations, thereby minimizing friction with the underlying cortex.
source: De-stretched cells displayed numerous bud-shaped evaginations at their apical PM side that correlated with the bright spots seen by fluorescence (Figure 1B and C), showing that the PM bends outward (thereby minimizing friction with the underlying cortex).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed outward bending direction of evaginations.

claim: Compression-induced evaginations have an average neck diameter of 83 nm and head diameter of 115 nm.
source: Analysis of the shape profile of compression-induced evaginations yielded an average diameter in the neck (cylindrical shape) of 83 nm and of 115 nm in the head (spherical shape), and average curvatures of 0.03 and 0.02 nm–1, respectively (Figure 1E, F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM measurements and analysis shown in Figures 1E, F, and G.

claim: Compression-induced evaginations have average curvatures of 0.03 nm⁻¹ at the neck and 0.02 nm⁻¹ at the head.
source: Analysis of the shape profile of compression-induced evaginations yielded an average diameter in the neck (cylindrical shape) of 83 nm and of 115 nm in the head (spherical shape), and average curvatures of 0.03 and 0.02 nm–1, respectively (Figure 1E, F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM measurements and analysis shown in Figures 1E, F, and G.

claim: Passive fold formation is followed by active resorption involving actin cytoskeleton rearrangements, allowing for topography equilibration within minutes.
source: In cells, passive fold formation is followed by active resorption involving actin cytoskeleton rearrangements, allowing for topography equilibration within minutes (Kosmalska et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work and by experimental observations in the current study.

claim: Full reabsorption of evaginations in NHDF leads to an average decay constant of 0.04 s⁻¹, corresponding to a half-life of about 17 seconds.
source: Here for NHDF, full reabsorption of evaginations leads to an average decay constant of 0.04 s–1 (corresponding to a half-life of about 17 s ensuring a complete return to fluorescent baseline at the end of the experiment).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of fluorescence decay curves from experimental data.

claim: Actin is recruited to evaginations with a delay relative to membrane marker appearance.
source: Actin recruitment was indeed delayed with respect to the membrane (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing temporal differences in fluorescence peaks shown in Figures 2F and G.

claim: Ezrin is recruited to evaginations with a delay of 10 seconds relative to the membrane marker.
source: fluorescence analysis of PM and Ezrin markers revealed a recruitment of the protein that mimicked, with a delay of 10 s, the one seen with actin (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence analysis shown in Figures 2I and J.

claim: I-BAR domain containing proteins have the ability to sense negative curvature and concomitantly recruit actin nucleation promoting factors or directly bind actin monomers.
source: I-BAR domain containing proteins have the ability to sense negative curvature, corresponding to an extruded PM, and to concomitantly recruit actin nucleation promoting factors (NPFs) or even directly bind actin monomers (Simunovic et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on I-BAR protein properties.

claim: Ezrin needs to act in partnership with the I-BAR protein IRSp53 to enrich in negatively curved membranes.
source: Interestingly, a recent work described how Ezrin needs to act in partnership with the I-BAR protein IRSp53 to enrich in negatively curved membranes (Tsai et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Tsai et al., 2018.

claim: The I-BAR domain of IRSp53 displays a peak of sorting at evaginations with curvatures of 0.05 nm⁻¹.
source: Moreover, recent studies in vitro and in vivo showed that the I-BAR domain of IRSp53 displays a peak of sorting at evaginations with curvatures of 0.05 nm–1.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to recent studies on IRSp53 curvature sensing.

claim: Curvature values comparable to those obtained by TEM imaging of evaginations lead to a twofold enrichment of the IRSp53 I-BAR domain with respect to a control membrane marker.
source: They also revealed that lower curvature values comparable to the ones obtained by TEM imaging of our evaginations led to a twofold enrichment of this domain with respect to a control membrane marker (Prévost et al., 2015; Breuer et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Prévost et al., 2015 and Breuer et al., 2019.

claim: No significant differences in decay curves were observed between wild-type MEF cells and IRSp53 null MEF cells.
source: To investigate this possibility, we used isogenic MEFs isolated from IRSp53 null mice (Disanza et al., 2013; Weiss et al., 2009; Sawallisch et al., 2009) that we call IRSp53-/- cells, and compared their decay curves with wild-type (WT) MEF cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C). No significant differences were observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison of decay curves shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: IRSp53 is enriched at plasma membrane evaginations generated by stretch release.
source: We analyzed the PM evaginations generated by a stretch-release cycle and found an increase in APEX signal to evaginations only in IRSp53-FL-transfected cells (Figure 3A), but not in control mito-GFP-transfected cells (Figure 3B). These findings strongly suggest that IRSp53 is recruited to the evaginations.
evidence: The claim is supported by APEX-TEM imaging data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: mRNA levels of I-BAR proteins IRTKs and MIM are robustly upregulated in IRSp53-/- cells.
source: Consistently, we found that the mRNA levels of the I-BAR proteins IRTKs and MIM were robustly upregulated in the IRSp53-/- cells, while MIM was elevated in the IRSP53-/- IRTKs KO cell line (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Cells genetically knocked out for IRSp53 adapt to the loss of protein by compensatory elevation of I-BAR family proteins.
source: Thus, cells genetically knocked out for IRSp53 adapt to the loss of protein by compensatory elevation of I-BAR family protein, implying that stable KO strategies are not suited to clarify the overall role of I-BAR protein in evagination resorption.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed upregulation of other I-BAR proteins in knockout cells.

claim: IRSp53 full-length protein colocalizes with the plasma membrane and its fluorescence in evaginations is significantly delayed with respect to the membrane marker.
source: We started by overexpressing EGFP-IRSP53-FL protein in IRSp53-/-R cells which colocalized with the PM (Video 4). Further confirming IRSP53 recruitment to the invagination, protein fluorescence in the evagination was significantly delayed with respect to the PM marker (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figures 3E-F and Video 4.

claim: Multiple protein interaction domains of IRSp53, in addition to the I-BAR, mediate the association with the plasma membrane.
source: Next, we used the fluorescently labeled mutants, which all colocalized with the PM marker (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–G), indicating that multiple protein interaction domains of IRSp53, in addition to the I-BAR, mediate the association with the PM, as already suggested in previous studies (Robens et al., 2010; Bisi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with IRSp53 mutants and by citation to previous studies.

claim: EGFP-IRSP53-4KE and IRSP53-I268N mutants do not affect plasma membrane decay constants and lag times when compared with IRSp53-FL.
source: Notably, the EGFP-IRSP53-4KE and IRSP53-I268N did not affect PM decay constants and lag times when compared with IRSp53-FL (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D and Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: Point mutants I403P and W413G in the SH3 domain have a small effect on resorption decay constant but significantly increase the lag time.
source: Specifically, the point mutant I403P and W413G in the SH3 domain had a small effect on resorption decay constant but significantly increased the lag time.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of decay constants and lag times for these mutants.

claim: Deletion of the entire I-BAR domain or overexpression of the I-BAR domain alone significantly impacts both the resorption decay constant and lag time.
source: The deletion of the entire I-BAR domain (Figure 3H, I) or the overexpression of the I-BAR domain alone significantly impacted, instead, both the resorption decay constant and lag time (also see Videos 7–10).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figures 3H and I.

claim: Impaired resorption correlates with delayed recruitment of IRSp53 mutants.
source: When all mutants were compared, impaired resorption (i.e., decreased decay constant) correlated with delayed recruitment (i.e., increased lag, Figure 3I and J and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, D, G, H). The more IRSp53 recruitment was delayed with respect to the PM marker, the less efficient the resorption was.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figures 3I, J and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of constitutively active Rac1-G12V accelerates evagination resorption significantly.
source: Confirming the involvement of Rac1, the expression of Rac1-G12V accelerated evagination resorption significantly whereas Rac1-T17N slowed it down in NHDF (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with Rac1 mutants shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2I-K.

claim: Expression of dominant negative Rac1-T17N slows down evagination resorption in NHDF.
source: Confirming the involvement of Rac1, the expression of Rac1-G12V accelerated evagination resorption significantly whereas Rac1-T17N slowed it down in NHDF (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with Rac1 mutants shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2I-K.

claim: IRSp53 has been described to promote Arp2/3-mediated actin polymerization driven by nucleation promoting factors WASP or WAVEs.
source: IRSp53 has been described to promote Arp2/3-mediated actin polymerization, which is driven by NPFs (WASP or WAVEs), both acting as an upstream (Connolly et al., 2005; Funato et al., 2004) and downstream regulator of the small GTPase Rac1.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Connolly et al., 2005 and Funato et al., 2004.

claim: Treatment with 10 µM of the N-WASP inhibitor Wiskostatin does not modify evagination resorption.
source: First, cell treatment with 10 µM of the N-WASP inhibitor Wiskostatin (Tsujita et al., 2015) reduced filopodia number as expected (Yang et al., 2020; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), but did not modify evagination resorption (Figure 4A, E, and F and Video 11).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with Wiskostatin treatment shown in Figures 4A, E, F.

claim: Treatment with 15 μM of the formin inhibitor SMIFH2 does not affect evagination resorption.
source: Second, treatment with 15 μM of the formin inhibitor SMIFH2 (Rizvi et al., 2009) reduced the number of filopodia as expected (Wakayama et al., 2015; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D), but did not affect evagination resorption either (Figure 4B, G, and H and Video 12).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with SMIFH2 treatment shown in Figures 4B, G, H.

claim: Treatment with 10 μM of the myosin II inhibitor Para-nitroblebbistatin does not impair evagination resorption.
source: Third, treatment with 10 μM of the myosin II inhibitor Para-nitroblebbistatin (Képiró et al., 2014) affected the integrity of stress fibers as expected (Tojkander et al., 2012, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) but did not impair evagination resorption (Figure 4C, I, and J and Video 13).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with Para-nitroblebbistatin treatment shown in Figures 4C, I, J.

claim: Treatment with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK-666 significantly reduces evagination resorption.
source: Conversely the treatment with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK-666 (Hetrick et al., 2013) significantly reduced evagination resorption in comparison to DMSO-treated controls (Figure 4D, K, and L and Video 14).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with CK-666 treatment shown in Figures 4D, K, L.

claim: WAVE2 is enriched at evagination sites relative to adjacent flat membrane.
source: With this, we calculated the increase in fluorescence between the evagination and adjacent flat membrane, in both WAVE and membrane markers. This increase was higher for WAVE than for the membrane, indicating a relative enrichment of WAVE at the evagination site (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Silencing of NCKAP1 (Nap1) increases the number of evaginations remaining after 25 seconds of resorption.
source: Confirming the role of the WRC, the number of evaginations remaining after 25 s of resorption was higher in cells with silenced Nap1 (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEM imaging and quantification shown in Figures 5C-E.

claim: Evagination resorption involves the enrichment of I-BAR proteins and WRCs, leading to actin polymerization in a myosin-independent and Arp2/3-dependent manner.
source: We conclude that evagination resorption upon compression involves the enrichment of I-BAR proteins and WRCs, leading to actin polymerization in a myosin-independent and Arp2/3-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental results including inhibitor studies and protein localization data.

claim: Previous work on IRSp53-mediated actin polymerization describes the extension of out-of-plane protrusions in the form of filopodia or lamellipodia as a result of out-of-plane polymerization forces pushing against the plasma membrane.
source: Previous work on IRSp53-mediated actin polymerization describes the extension of out-of-plane protrusions in the form of filopodia or lamellipodia (Prévost et al., 2015; Disanza et al., 2006; Connolly et al., 2005; Lim et al., 2008; Goh et al., 2012; Kast and Dominguez, 2019) as a result of out-of-plane polymerization forces pushing against the PM (Gov, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to multiple previous studies.

claim: Polymerization of an actin cortex retracts and flattens cellular blebs through a mechanism that depends on myosin contractility.
source: At larger scales, polymerization of an actin cortex retracts and flattens cellular blebs, but this mechanism depends on myosin contractility (Charras et al., 2006), and hence is not applicable here.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Charras et al., 2006.

claim: The theoretical model predicts that curvature-sensitive I-BAR proteins become enriched in the evagination within a second following its generation.
source: Following the generation of a membrane evagination by buckling-induced delamination (Kosmalska et al., 2015; Staykova et al., 2013), our model predicts that curvature-sensitive I-BAR proteins become enriched in the evagination within a second (magenta colormap in Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical modeling results shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The lateral tension gradient induced by localized polymerization induces a centrifugal cortical flow which frictionally drags the inextensible membrane outward favoring flattening.
source: In contrast, the lateral tension gradient induces a centrifugal cortical flow (black arrows), which frictionally drags the inextensible membrane outward favoring flattening.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical modeling results.

claim: The predicted relative trends of plasma membrane and regulator densities from the model match experimental observations when comparing plasma membrane and actin or Ezrin.
source: Whereas predicted actin flows occur at a scale well below the diffraction limit and can therefore not be observed experimentally, the predicted relative trends of PM and regulator densities match our experimental observations when comparing PM and actin (Figure 2G) or Ezrin (Figure 2J).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison between model predictions and experimental data shown in Figures 2G and 2J.

claim: Model predictions are consistent with the observation that evagination resorption is impaired when inhibiting Arp2/3 or WRC but not myosin or formin activity.
source: Predictions are also consistent with our observation that evagination resorption is impaired when inhibiting Arp2/3 (Figure 4L) or WRC (Figure 5E) but not myosin or formin activity (Figure 4H and J).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison between model predictions and experimental data from inhibitor studies.

claim: The mechanism is based on a local gradient in extensile versus contractile behavior around the evagination, and hence should depend on Arp2/3 but not on formin or myosin.
source: Indeed, the mechanism is based on a local gradient in extensile versus contractile behavior around the evagination, and hence it should depend on Arp2/3 (which acts locally at the evagination) and not on formin or myosin, which would regulate overall contractility levels and not specifically local gradients.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the theoretical model mechanism.

claim: IRSp53 mediates the resorption rather than formation of membrane curvature in the context of compression-induced evaginations.
source: Notably, we show that IRSp53 mediates the resorption rather than formation of membrane curvature, as previously described in the context of filopodia extension (Disanza et al., 2013) and HIV budding (Inamdar et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and contrasted with previous work cited.

claim: The role of IRSp53 is visible through dominant-negative effects of its mutants but not through overexpression or depletion.
source: Indeed, the role of IRSp53 is visible through dominant-negative effects of its mutants but not through overexpression or depletion, suggesting that I-BAR proteins with similar function (such as IRTKs) are likely to play compensatory or redundant roles.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results with IRSp53 mutants and knockout cells.

claim: IRSp53 in complex with WAVE has been described to localize to saddle curvatures which occur at the neck of invaginations.
source: IRSp53 in complex with WAVE has also been described to localize to saddle curvatures (Pipathsouk et al., 2021), which occur at the neck of invaginations.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Pipathsouk et al., 2021.

claim: Cell compression upon a stretch cycle triggers endocytosis through the CLIC-GEEC but not the clathrin-mediated pathway.
source: Beyond the formation of evaginations, we previously showed that cell compression upon a stretch cycle also triggers endocytosis through the CLIC-GEEC (but not the clathrin-mediated) pathway (Thottacherry et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Thottacherry et al., 2018.

claim: IRSp53 has been described to regulate the CLIC-GEEC endocytic pathway.
source: In turn, IRSp53 has been described to regulate the CLIC-GEEC endocytic pathway (Sathe et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Sathe et al., 2018.

claim: The I268N-CRIB and 4KE-I-BAR IRSp53 mutants strongly impaired endocytosis but did not affect evagination resorption.
source: First, the I268N-CRIB and 4KE-I-BAR IRSp53 mutants strongly impaired endocytosis (Sathe et al., 2018), but did not affect evagination resorption (Figure 3J), showing that IRSp53 affects these processes through different mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J and by citation to previous work.

claim: The sites of evaginations and of endocytic buds do not coincide.
source: Second, as we previously determined, the sites of evaginations and of endocytic buds do not coincide (Thottacherry et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Thottacherry et al., 2018.

claim: Upon cell compression, cells use caveolae formation and the CLIC-GEEC endocytic pathway to store material from the plasma membrane and recover resting tension.
source: Thus, our findings unveil a novel mechanosensing mechanism: upon cell compression, cells are known to use caveolae formation (Sinha et al., 2011) and the CLIC-GEEC endocytic pathway (Thottacherry et al., 2018) to store material from the PM and recover resting tension.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Sinha et al., 2011 and Thottacherry et al., 2018.

claim: Plasma membrane flattening in response to mechanical perturbations involves the IRSp53-Rac1-Arp2/3 network.
source: To achieve PM flattening in response to mechanical perturbations, cells employ the IRSp53-Rac1-Arp2/3 network, which has been well described to polymerize actin in the context of lamellipodia extension or ruffling (Teodorof et al., 2009; Suraneni et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and by citation to previous work.

claim: The mechanism involves lamellipodial rather than filopodial formation.
source: Thus, this involves lamellipodial rather than filopodial formation, which is consistent with our previous observation that IRSp53 does not recruit the formin nucleator mDia (Disanza et al., 2013) during initial filopodia formation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations and citation to previous work.

claim: The stretch/compression stimuli occur at the scale of seconds, while subsequent resorption occurs at the scale of minutes.
source: In our experiments, the stretch/compression stimuli occur at the scale of seconds, while subsequent resorption occurs at the scale of minutes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of the time scales involved.

claim: Similar stretch-compression situations could include fast compressions of cells embedded in connective tissues or apical expansion and contractions of amnioserosa cells during dorsal closure in Drosophila embryos.
source: In vivo, similar situations could include for instance the fast compressions of cells embedded in connective tissues (Zhao et al., 2020), or the apical expansion and contractions of amnioserosa cells during dorsal closure in Drosophila embryos (Jayasinghe et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting potential physiological scenarios based on citation to previous work.

claim: Other scenarios where the mechanism could be relevant include responses to wounding, contraction in muscle cells, or contractile pulling during fibroblast migration.
source: Other scenarios could include responses to wounding (Agha et al., 2011), contraction in muscle cells, or contractile pulling during fibroblast migration (Plotnikov et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting potential physiological scenarios based on citation to previous work.
